paragraphs: Evaluating stereotyping in language models requires knowing which stereotypes matter in the societies where those models are used. The paper argues that existing evaluation resources do not adequately represent diverse local perspectives, particularly the experiences of marginalized identities. As a result, assessments can underestimate harm or give a distorted picture of its distribution.

The authors develop a community-engaged approach to expanding stereotype evaluation resources in the Indian social context. Their work includes axes of disparity specific to India and adds more than 1,000 stereotypes across numerous identities. Community participation connects the resource-building process to locally situated experiences rather than relying solely on the coverage of existing evaluations.

The paper also demonstrates that the expanded resource is useful for evaluating language models. Its contribution is both a concrete collection and an example of how evaluation coverage can become more culturally informed. The stated result concerns improved resources for measuring stereotyping; it does not establish that the evaluated models themselves become less harmful.
neurips-2023-building-socio-culturally-i.tldr: Community engagement adds over 1,000 India-context stereotypes to resources for more culturally informed language-model evaluation.

paragraphs: Programmatic weak supervision and semi-supervised learning both address the expense of labeling training data. Weak supervision supplies labels programmatically, while semi-supervised learning makes use of unlabeled examples alongside labeled ones. Their combination has produced increasingly complicated methods, making it difficult to determine which components actually justify their additional training cost.

The paper introduces a simple, modular design space for studying these combinations systematically. Within that space, relatively simple methods match the performance of more complex state-of-the-art approaches. Across eight standard weak-supervision benchmarks, the authors report an average three-percentage-point increase in accuracy or F1 score, alongside guidance about when additional components are worthwhile.

A central finding is that semi-supervised learning is unnecessary for attaining the best performance on most of the benchmarks examined. It becomes more useful when the final predictive model is smaller or when weak supervision labels only a small fraction of examples. These findings make model size and label coverage practical considerations when deciding whether added training complexity is beneficial.
neurips-2023-characterizing-the-impacts-.tldr: Simple weak-supervision methods can match complex alternatives, with semi-supervised learning especially useful for smaller models and sparse label coverage.

paragraphs: Comparing deepfake detectors becomes unreliable when each method receives differently processed data or is assessed under different experimental rules. A performance difference may then reflect the evaluation setup as well as the detector. DeepfakeBench addresses this problem by providing a shared framework for implementing and evaluating detection methods consistently.

The benchmark combines unified data management, integrated implementations, and standardized evaluation metrics and protocols. Its modular codebase includes 15 detection methods and nine deepfake datasets, together with evaluation procedures and analysis tools. These components make consistent inputs and comparable assessments part of the benchmark itself, supporting more transparent and reproducible comparisons.

Beyond assembling the framework, the authors conduct extensive evaluations and analyze factors including data augmentation and model backbones. The abstract reports that these analyses produce additional insights without specifying a single winning configuration. Publicly available code, evaluations, and analyses make the contribution a reusable research resource: researchers can examine detector behavior within a common experimental setting and extend that setting with further methods.
neurips-2023-deepfakebench-a-comprehensi.tldr: DeepfakeBench standardizes data handling, detector implementations, and evaluation to make deepfake-detection comparisons more reproducible.

paragraphs: Learning several tasks at once creates an optimization problem in which improvements to different objectives can pull updates in competing directions. This paper proposes choosing a common descent direction while regularizing it toward a direction that improves a chosen linear combination of objectives. That combination can represent average performance or place greater emphasis on selected tasks.

The formulation includes gradient descent and the multiple-gradient descent algorithm as special cases. It leads to SDMGrad, which uses simple stochastic-gradient-style updates, and SDMGrad-OS, which samples objectives for efficiency. The authors analyze convergence across different choices of loop size and regularization strength, connecting algorithm design to the desired control over update direction.

Both methods improve sample-complexity guarantees for reaching an approximately Pareto-stationary point while remaining close to a conflict-avoidant direction. With a constant permitted distance from that direction, they match the best-known O(ε⁻²) complexity without assuming bounded function values. Experiments on supervised multi-task learning and reinforcement learning show competitive or improved performance relative to existing gradient-manipulation approaches.
neurips-2023-direction-oriented-multi-ob.tldr: SDMGrad offers simple stochastic updates with convergence guarantees for balancing multiple objectives and controlling conflicts between their update directions.

paragraphs: DreamWaltz tackles the combined challenge of generating a detailed three-dimensional avatar and making it move. Its inputs include text guidance and a parametric human-body prior. This body information gives the generation process a structural starting point, while the text specifies the avatar that the system should create.

For generation, the framework introduces an occlusion-aware, three-dimensionally consistent form of Score Distillation Sampling. It optimizes an implicit neural representation in a canonical pose and uses skeleton conditioning to align supervision with the current view. The authors present this alignment as a way to generate complex avatars while avoiding artifacts such as multiple faces.

For animation, DreamWaltz learns from diffusion-model image priors conditioned on different poses. The resulting representation can animate complex avatars without rigging or retraining for each requested pose. Evaluations support its effectiveness across varied shapes, appearances, and novel poses. The framework also supports more elaborate compositions involving interactions between avatars, objects, and scenes, extending its use beyond generating isolated characters.
neurips-2023-dreamwaltz-make-a-scene-wit.tldr: DreamWaltz combines text, body structure, and pose-conditioned diffusion guidance to create complex 3D avatars that can be animated without retraining.

paragraphs: Equivariant models change their outputs consistently when inputs undergo specified transformations. One way to obtain this behavior from an existing model is to combine features extracted from transformed inputs. The authors find that simply averaging those features, as equitune does, performs poorly on equivariant zero-shot tasks despite working well after fine-tuning.

Their explanation is a hypothesis: pretrained models may produce better features for some transformations than for others, so equal averaging can dilute useful information. The proposed λ-equitune instead learns importance weights through a small neural network. The authors prove that this construction is equivariant and can universally approximate equivariant functions.

They also adapt an optimization-based approach with suitable losses, calling it equizero. Both equitune and equizero fit within the λ-equitune framework. Experiments cover image classification, deep Q-learning, fairness in language generation, and compositional language generalization. The reported zero-shot and fine-tuning results support weighted feature combination as a broadly useful transfer strategy, with λ-equitune outperforming equitune in the evaluations.
neurips-2023-efficient-equivariant-trans.tldr: λ-equitune learns how to weight transformed-input features, improving equivariant transfer while retaining formal equivariance and approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: A bandit learner chooses actions while learning which ones produce better rewards. This paper studies a setting where each reward arrives with additional feedback correlated with it. For example, a service recommendation platform may observe both a user's rating and the service's delivery time. The additional observation offers information beyond the reward alone.

The authors develop a reward estimator that uses this auxiliary feedback and comes with tight confidence bounds. These bounds quantify uncertainty in the reward estimates used for learning. The proposed method achieves smaller regret, meaning less accumulated loss from choosing actions that fall short of the best available choices.

The theoretical analysis expresses the reduction in regret in terms of the correlation coefficient between rewards and auxiliary feedback. This makes the relationship between the two observations central to understanding the benefit, rather than treating any extra measurement as equally valuable. Experiments across different settings also show performance gains, supporting the proposed use of correlated feedback within the parameterized bandit framework.
neurips-2023-exploiting-correlated-auxil.tldr: Correlated auxiliary observations improve reward estimation in parameterized bandits, with regret reductions characterized by their correlation with rewards.

paragraphs: Bayesian bandit analysis evaluates learning performance over problem instances drawn from a prior distribution. The paper studies Bayes regret, which measures accumulated decision loss under that averaging. Its main contribution is finite-time upper bounds with logarithmic dependence on the number of rounds, substantially sharpening the square-root-style guarantees commonly used in this literature.

For an upper confidence bound algorithm in multi-armed bandits, the authors obtain bounds of O(cΔ log n) and O(ch log² n). The constants capture information about reward gaps in instances drawn from the prior and about the prior distribution itself. The second bound asymptotically matches a known lower bound, connecting a finite-time guarantee to an established limit.

The authors also apply their proof techniques to linear bandits to demonstrate their broader applicability. Their analysis distinguishes two roles for a prior: it defines how performance is averaged, and it can supply information to the learner. This distinction helps clarify how prior knowledge enters Bayesian learning guarantees and why the resulting bounds can be substantially tighter.
neurips-2023-finite-time-logarithmic-bay.tldr: The paper proves finite-time logarithmic and squared-logarithmic Bayes regret bounds and extends its analysis to linear bandits.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient methods improve a reinforcement-learning policy by estimating how changes to it affect performance. The paper examines a fundamental obstacle to this approach: for certain classes of decision processes, the objective over policies can be so irregular that a gradient does not exist. In those settings, improving the gradient estimate alone cannot resolve the underlying problem.

The authors use ideas from chaos theory and nonsmooth analysis to characterize these landscapes. Their analysis considers maximal Lyapunov exponents and Hölder exponents, connecting the behavior of the underlying system with the smoothness of the policy objective. This provides a framework for studying when policy optimization encounters extremely rough or fractal structure.

They also introduce a practical procedure for estimating local objective smoothness from samples. Such an estimate can help identify when training has reached a fractal region. Experiments illustrate how this phenomenon explains some policy-optimization failures. The claim is specifically about certain problem classes and failure cases, providing one explanation for unsuccessful training rather than a universal account of reinforcement-learning difficulties.
neurips-2023-fractal-landscapes-in-polic.tldr: Some policy objectives have fractal landscapes without usable gradients, and the paper provides analysis and a sample-based diagnostic for this failure mode.

paragraphs: Vision-and-language navigation requires an agent to connect verbal instructions with what it sees while moving through an environment. This paper investigates that matching process through the Fourier domain, which separates visual information by spatial frequency. The authors provide evidence that high-frequency information plays an important role in matching visual observations to language.

They use this finding to design Frequency-enhanced Data Augmentation, or FDA. During training, the agent encounters environments in which only some high-frequency visual information corresponds to its instructions. The intended effect is selective attention to the relevant information: the agent must learn which high-frequency features support the instruction rather than simply responding to all of them.

Experiments on R2R, RxR, CVDN, and REVERIE show performance improvements when FDA is incorporated into existing navigation approaches. The technique adds no model parameters, so the reported gains come through the training-data augmentation rather than an enlarged model. Together, the findings identify frequency-sensitive visual-textual matching as a useful target for improving instruction-following navigation.
neurips-2023-frequency-enhanced-data-aug.tldr: FDA improves instruction-following navigation by training agents to select relevant high-frequency visual information without adding model parameters.

paragraphs: Classification models often optimize a surrogate loss, such as cross-entropy, instead of directly minimizing classification mistakes. H-consistency bounds connect the resulting surrogate-loss estimation error to zero-one estimation error within a specified hypothesis set. Because these guarantees are non-asymptotic and account for the model class, they offer information beyond eventual Bayes consistency.

Previously, establishing such bounds required separate arguments for individual losses. This paper develops general characterizations through explicitly defined error transformations. It derives new tight bounds for constrained losses and comp-sum losses, a family that includes the cross-entropy commonly applied to neural-network outputs. The framework gives a more unified way to analyze these relationships.

The authors also move beyond completeness assumptions used in earlier work to include bounded hypothesis sets that better reflect practical restrictions. Examples illustrate the general results. Their analysis identifies a previously derived multiclass cross-entropy guarantee as an uninformative excess bound and replaces it with a stronger one, improving what the theory says about the connection between training objectives and classification performance.
neurips-2023-h-consistency-bounds-charac.tldr: The paper develops general, tighter guarantees connecting surrogate-loss error to classification error within specified hypothesis classes.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets multiple parties train a shared model while retaining their data locally. For visual recognition, differences between clients' data can make matching centralized training difficult. This paper examines architectural design as an important part of that challenge, arguing that conclusions drawn from shallow or simple networks may transfer poorly to larger recognition systems.

The study evaluates models from five architectural families on four federated-learning datasets, including convolutional networks, transformers, and MLP-mixers. It investigates how these choices affect performance under heterogeneous data. It also revisits the weaker performance of convolution-based architectures in federated settings and studies the influence of normalization layers.

The experiments show that architecture can substantially improve federated visual-recognition performance and narrow the gap with centralized learning. This makes the model itself an important design choice when evaluating federated methods, alongside the collaborative training procedure. The findings support studying architectures representative of practical visual-recognition systems, since a result obtained with a simplified network may not capture how a larger model behaves.
neurips-2023-handling-data-heterogeneity.tldr: Experiments across five architecture families show that model design can substantially improve federated visual recognition under heterogeneous client data.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning theory often studies small state-action spaces or relatively simple value functions, even though practical applications can be much more complex. Kernel methods offer a way to represent nonlinear value functions in larger spaces. This paper develops π-KRVI, an optimistic version of least-squares value iteration whose action-value function belongs to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space.

The main contribution is a regret analysis that improves on earlier guarantees by a polynomial factor in the number of episodes. Regret tracks the accumulated performance shortfall during learning. A sublinear bound means this accumulated shortfall grows more slowly than the number of episodes, providing a meaningful guarantee of improving average performance.

The improvement is particularly consequential for highly nonsmooth kernels, including the Neural Tangent kernel and some Matérn kernels. Earlier results gave superlinear bounds for these cases, whereas the new analysis gives sublinear regret. Where matching lower bounds are known, including the mentioned kernel cases, the upper bounds are order optimal. That qualification ties the optimality claim to established limits.
neurips-2023-kernelized-reinforcement-le.tldr: π-KRVI provides sharper kernelized reinforcement-learning regret bounds, achieving order-optimal rates in cases with known lower bounds.

paragraphs: Language models need a connection to visual information to support tasks such as visual question answering. Building that connection commonly involves expensive image-text alignment training. Language-Quantized AutoEncoder, or LQAE, explores an unsupervised alternative that uses a pretrained language model to help organize image representations without aligned image-text pairs.

LQAE modifies a vector-quantized autoencoder by quantizing image embeddings with a pretrained language codebook. This expresses an image through a sequence of text-associated tokens. A masked version of those embeddings is then passed through a language-model denoiser such as BERT as part of reconstructing the original input. Similar images consequently learn representations involving similar clusters of text tokens.

The resulting image tokens support few-shot multimodal learning with large language models. The authors report improvements over baseline methods on tasks including image classification and visual question answering, using as few as one to ten image-text pairs. These pairs belong to the few-shot use of the learned representations; the alignment approach itself does not require paired image-text training data.
neurips-2023-language-quantized-autoenco.tldr: LQAE learns text-aligned image tokens without paired alignment data, enabling multimodal few-shot learning with as few as one to ten image-text pairs.

paragraphs: Domain-adaptive object detection transfers a detector from labeled source images to an unlabeled target domain. Existing approaches often concentrate on adapting the visual backbone that extracts image features. This paper highlights a second source of mismatch: the detection head that turns those features into detections can also carry domain-specific bias.

DA-Pro combines a vision-language-model backbone with a detection head generated through learnable, domain-adaptive prompts. Each prompt includes shared tokens, domain-specific tokens, and a textual description of the domain alongside the class label. Two constraints across source and target domains encourage the prompts to capture both common knowledge and information particular to each domain.

The framework also ensembles prompts to reduce sensitivity to prompt disturbance. Across multiple adaptation tasks, the experiments show that the learned prompts produce useful domain-related detection heads and improve detection performance. The approach therefore expands where adaptation happens: a robust feature extractor is paired with a head that can reflect the domain in which detection is performed.
neurips-2023-learning-domain-aware-detec.tldr: DA-Pro uses domain-adaptive prompts to generate detection heads that capture shared and domain-specific knowledge for cross-domain object detection.

paragraphs: As AI systems take part in decisions with ethical consequences, the paper asks how moral responsibility can be defined in a form applicable to them. It begins with two familiar requirements: an agent's action must cause the outcome, and the agent must have had some awareness of the action's possible moral consequences.

The contribution is a formal definition of both requirements within causal models. The causal condition addresses the relationship between an action and an outcome. The epistemic condition addresses what the agent was aware of. Treating these separately makes both causal involvement and awareness explicit parts of the proposed account of responsibility.

The author compares this definition with the approaches of Braham and van Hees and of Halpern and Kleiman-Weiner. The account is then generalized to represent a degree of responsibility, allowing more than a yes-or-no judgment. The paper's stated contribution is thus conceptual and formal: it provides a framework for expressing responsibility and comparing accounts of it in settings involving AI systems.
neurips-2023-moral-responsibility-for-ai.tldr: The paper formalizes causal involvement and awareness as conditions for moral responsibility, then extends the definition to degrees of responsibility.

paragraphs: Text descriptions and example images offer complementary ways to specify which objects a detector should find. Text supports open-vocabulary categories, while visual examples can express finer distinctions in appearance. MQ-Det combines both forms of category query to support detection across unfamiliar categories and different levels of descriptive detail.

The method adds a gated, class-scalable perceiver module to an existing frozen language-queried detector. This module supplements category text with visual information for each class. A vision-conditioned masked-language prediction strategy addresses the learning inertia associated with the frozen detector. The architecture is designed to work with most language-queried detectors, making the addition broadly reusable.

The experiments show substantial benefits from multimodal queries. For GLIP, the authors report a 7.8% AP improvement on LVIS without downstream fine-tuning and an average 6.3% AP improvement across 13 few-shot downstream tasks. They report only 3% additional modulating time relative to GLIP. These results support adding visual exemplars as an efficient way to enrich what category queries communicate.
neurips-2023-multi-modal-queried-object-.tldr: MQ-Det enriches text-queried detectors with visual examples, improving open-world and few-shot detection with modest additional modulating time.

paragraphs: Multiple sequence alignments organize related protein sequences and contain biological information useful for protein structure prediction and design. Models such as AlphaFold2 make extensive use of these alignments. Producing them requires substantial computation, however, and the lack of publicly available training collections comparable to AlphaFold2's has constrained research access.

OpenProteinSet addresses this resource gap with an open-source collection of more than 16 million multiple sequence alignments. The corpus also includes associated structural homologs from the Protein Data Bank and protein-structure predictions from AlphaFold2. Bringing these resources together provides large-scale material for research connecting protein sequences with structural information.

The authors point to a concrete demonstration of usefulness: they previously retrained AlphaFold2 successfully using OpenProteinSet. They also anticipate applications as training and validation data for protein structure, function, and design, as well as multimodal machine learning. Those broader uses are presented as expected opportunities. The established contribution is the accessible corpus and its demonstrated support for retraining a major structure-prediction model.
neurips-2023-openproteinset-training-dat.tldr: OpenProteinSet releases over 16 million protein sequence alignments with structural information and has supported successful AlphaFold2 retraining.

paragraphs: Can a mean estimator automatically exploit favorable properties of a distribution to outperform guarantees designed for the worst case? This paper gives a qualified answer: improvement is possible in limited regimes, but not generally. It studies this question assuming only that the distribution has a finite mean, without supplying additional structural information.

The core construction creates another distribution whose mean is well separated from the original, yet which cannot be reliably distinguished from it with the specified sample size and confidence. This alternative preserves whichever moments are finite; when variance exists, its variance is at most twice the original's. The ambiguity limits how accurately an estimator can adapt to apparently favorable data.

The authors conclude that no reasonable estimator can asymptotically beat the sub-Gaussian error rate by more than constant factors for any distribution. They introduce neighborhood optimality to formalize a useful middle ground between overly demanding instance optimality and weak admissibility. Median-of-means is neighborhood optimal up to constants; removing that constant-factor slack remains open.
neurips-2023-optimality-in-mean-estimati.tldr: Indistinguishable nearby distributions limit adaptive mean estimation, motivating a neighborhood-optimality framework in which median-of-means is optimal up to constants.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate samples through repeated denoising, making long sequences of dependent steps a sampling bottleneck. This paper explores accelerating those steps through parallel computation. Its central tradeoff is spending more compute to reduce elapsed time while retaining the denoising sequence, instead of relying solely on shortening that sequence.

ParaDiGMS uses Picard iterations to handle the apparent dependency problem. It guesses the results of future denoising steps, processes multiple steps in parallel, and repeatedly refines the guesses until convergence. The method applies to pretrained diffusion models and can also be combined with existing fast samplers such as DDIM and DPMSolver.

Across robotics and image-generation models, the authors report sampling speedups of two to four times. Reported sampling times include 0.2 seconds for a 100-step DiffusionPolicy and 14.6 seconds for 1,000-step StableDiffusion-v2. They observe no measurable degradation in task reward, FID, or CLIP score in these evaluations. The results demonstrate a practical compute-for-speed option while preserving the measured quality of the tested models.
neurips-2023-parallel-sampling-of-diffus.tldr: ParaDiGMS parallelizes diffusion sampling through iterative refinement, reporting two-to-fourfold speedups without measurable degradation on the evaluated metrics.

paragraphs: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning trains an agent to reach different goals using only previously collected data. Its theoretical analysis becomes difficult when the state space is large and the data cover only the policy of interest. This paper gives guarantees for a slightly modified version of an existing empirically successful algorithm.

The proof establishes sample complexity polynomial in the inverse of the desired policy suboptimality, up to logarithmic factors, with general function approximation. It relies on strong or semi-strong convexity of the objectives. The assumptions include single-policy concentrability, concerning dataset coverage of the relevant policy, and realizability, concerning the expressive adequacy of the chosen function class.

The algorithm separates training into two uninterleaved stages: V-learning and policy learning. It avoids minimax optimization, which the authors identify as supporting computational stability. Experiments in several real-world environments show that the modification outperforms the earlier algorithm. The contribution therefore combines a conditional efficiency guarantee under limited coverage assumptions with empirical evidence that the theoretically motivated change improves performance.
neurips-2023-provably-efficient-offline-.tldr: A modified offline goal-learning algorithm gains polynomial sample-complexity guarantees under single-policy coverage and realizability assumptions, alongside empirical improvements.

paragraphs: Post-training quantization compresses a trained language model by representing its weights with fewer bits. QuIP studies how to make extremely low-bit representations viable. Its central insight is that rounding behaves better when weight magnitudes are spread more evenly and the directions most sensitive to rounding are not aligned with individual coordinate axes.

The method combines adaptive rounding with efficient preprocessing and postprocessing. Random orthogonal transformations establish the desired incoherence in the weights and Hessian, which describes sensitivity in the quadratic approximation. The rounding procedure then minimizes a quadratic proxy objective. This links the representation change to an explicit approximation of the cost of quantization errors.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis for quantization at language-model scale and show that the theory also applies to OPTQ. Empirically, incoherence preprocessing improves several existing quantization algorithms. They report viable results at two bits per weight, presenting this as a first for LLM quantization. The finding supports both the full QuIP method and incoherence processing as a useful component for other quantizers.
neurips-2023-quip-2-bit-quantization-of-.tldr: QuIP combines random orthogonal transformations and adaptive rounding to achieve viable two-bit language-model quantization with theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: The paper compares which spatial frequencies humans and neural networks use to recognize objects. It applies critical band masking: adding noise within selected frequency bands and measuring the resulting recognition loss. Tests involve 14 humans and 76 neural networks performing 16-category ImageNet recognition, providing a shared task for examining frequency sensitivity.

Humans use a channel about one octave wide, matching earlier findings for letters and periodic patterns. Network channels are two to four times wider. Their sensitivity therefore extends to frequencies outside the human-sensitive range, where noise can impair networks while sparing human performance. This reveals a specific mismatch despite both systems performing object recognition.

Channel bandwidth, center frequency, and peak noise sensitivity together correlate strongly with shape bias and adversarial robustness, explaining 51% and 66% of variance respectively in the reported analyses. Adversarial training improves robustness but broadens channels further away from the human bandwidth. The authors suggest narrower channels might improve robustness; the evidence presents that as a possibility, rather than an established causal result.
neurips-2023-spatial-frequency-channels-.tldr: Neural networks respond to much broader spatial-frequency bands than humans, and adversarial training widens that mismatch despite improving robustness.

paragraphs: Non-Gaussian Component Analysis asks whether data that otherwise look Gaussian contain a hidden direction with a different distribution. The paper studies the difficulty of this problem in the Statistical Query model. In the setup considered, one direction follows a univariate distribution A, while the orthogonal directions follow a standard Gaussian.

Earlier hardness results required two properties of A. Its low-order moments had to match those of a Gaussian, and its chi-squared norm relative to the Gaussian had to be finite. Moment matching hides differences from low-order statistical information. The second restriction, however, was imposed for technical reasons in the earlier proof methodology.

The authors remove that second requirement and establish near-optimal Statistical Query lower bounds using moment matching alone. This broadens the distributions covered by the hardness theory and shows that finite chi-squared norm is unnecessary for the result. The contribution concerns limits within the specified query model, strengthening the theoretical basis of a methodology previously applied across multiple contexts.
neurips-2023-sq-lower-bounds-for-non-gau.tldr: Near-optimal Statistical Query hardness for Non-Gaussian Component Analysis requires moment matching without the earlier finite chi-squared-norm assumption.

paragraphs: Robots often struggle to manipulate articulated objects from unfamiliar categories because their shapes and meanings differ from those seen during training. Learning through a few interactions can help, but repeatedly exploring every new object instance is costly. Where2Explore instead aims to learn about a novel category through minimal interactions with a limited number of instances.

The framework builds on shared local geometry across otherwise different objects. Pullable handles and graspable edges can support similar actions even when the overall objects differ substantially. Where2Explore explicitly estimates geometric similarity, transfers affordance knowledge to familiar-looking parts, and identifies unfamiliar local regions as targets for exploration.

This division directs interaction toward regions where existing knowledge is less applicable while reusing knowledge elsewhere. Experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate efficient few-shot exploration and generalization. The stated findings support local geometric similarity as a useful basis for learning new manipulation categories, reducing reliance on separate exploratory interactions with every unseen instance.
neurips-2023-where2explore-few-shot-affo.tldr: Where2Explore transfers manipulation knowledge across similar object parts and focuses a few exploratory interactions on unfamiliar geometry.
